organizations.name: United States Preventive Services Task Force
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology

recommendations.title: Colorectal Cancer Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for colorectal cancer in all adults aged 45 to 75 years. The decision to screen adults aged 76 to 85 years should be individualized.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 45–75 should be screened for colorectal cancer. Options include colonoscopy every 10 years, stool DNA test (Cologuard) every 1–3 years, or annual FIT/FOBT stool blood tests. Ask your doctor which is right for you.

recommendations.title: Breast Cancer Screening (Mammography)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for breast cancer with mammography every 2 years for women aged 40 to 74 years.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Women 40–74 should get a mammogram every 2 years. Women at higher risk due to dense breasts, family history, or genetic factors should talk with their doctor about additional screening.

recommendations.title: Breast Cancer Screening — ACS (Annual Starting at 40)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Women with average risk should have the opportunity to start annual mammography at age 40. All women should be offered annual mammography starting at 40. Women at high risk (BRCA mutation, strong family history, prior chest radiation) should have annual mammography and breast MRI starting at 30.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: The American Cancer Society recommends yearly mammograms starting at 40 for average-risk women — more frequent than the USPSTF recommendation. High-risk women (BRCA mutation or strong family history) should start annual mammogram plus MRI at age 30.

recommendations.title: Cervical Cancer Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for cervical cancer every 3 years with cervical cytology alone (Pap smear) in women aged 21 to 65. Women 30–65 may alternatively screen every 5 years with hrHPV testing alone or co-testing (Pap + HPV).
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Women 21–65 should be screened for cervical cancer. Ages 21–29: Pap smear every 3 years. Ages 30–65: Pap smear every 3 years, or HPV test alone every 5 years, or both together every 5 years.

recommendations.title: Lung Cancer Screening (Annual Low-Dose CT)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Annual low-dose CT (LDCT) scan for adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you're 50–80, smoked a pack a day for 20+ years, and currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years, ask your doctor about annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening. This is one of the most effective ways to catch lung cancer early.

recommendations.title: Prostate Cancer Screening (PSA) — Shared Decision Making
recommendations.recommendation_text: For men aged 55 to 69 years, the decision to undergo periodic PSA-based prostate cancer screening should be an individual one, made after discussion of potential benefits and harms with a clinician. Routine screening is not recommended for men 70 and older. Black men and those with a first-degree relative diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65 are at higher risk and may benefit from earlier discussion.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Men aged 55–69 should have an informed conversation with their doctor about PSA screening — it can detect cancer early but also leads to overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Black men or those whose father or brother had prostate cancer before age 65 are at higher risk and should consider discussing it earlier.

recommendations.title: BRCA-Related Cancer: Risk Assessment and Genetic Counseling
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen women who have a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer, or an ancestry associated with BRCA1/2 gene mutations, using a brief familial risk assessment tool. Refer women with a positive screen to genetic counseling and, if indicated, BRCA testing.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have a family history of breast or ovarian cancer — especially in close relatives or at young ages — or are of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, ask your doctor about BRCA risk assessment. Genetic counseling can clarify your risk and guide preventive options including enhanced surveillance or risk-reducing surgery.

recommendations.title: Skin Cancer Prevention: UV Counseling
recommendations.recommendation_text: Counsel fair-skinned persons aged 6 months to 24 years about minimizing ultraviolet radiation exposure to reduce the risk of skin cancer.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Children and young adults with fair skin should be counseled on sun protection — use sunscreen SPF 30+, wear protective clothing and hats, seek shade, and avoid tanning beds — to reduce lifetime skin cancer risk.

recommendations.title: Hypertension in Adults: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for hypertension in adults 18 years or older with office blood pressure measurement. Obtain measurements outside of the clinical setting for diagnostic confirmation before starting treatment.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All adults 18+ should have their blood pressure checked regularly. If it reads high at the doctor's office, home or ambulatory monitoring is recommended to confirm before starting treatment.

recommendations.title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: One-Time Ultrasound Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) with one-time abdominal duplex ultrasonography in men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked (at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime).
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked should get a one-time abdominal ultrasound to check for an enlarged aorta (abdominal aortic aneurysm). If found early, surveillance and possibly surgery can prevent a potentially fatal rupture.

recommendations.title: Lipid Panel for Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
recommendations.recommendation_text: Obtain a fasting lipid panel in all adults starting at age 20. Repeat every 4–6 years in adults 20–39 with no risk factors; every 1–2 years in those with elevated risk, known ASCVD, or on lipid-lowering therapy.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults should have their cholesterol checked starting at age 20. A fasting lipid panel measures total cholesterol, LDL (bad), HDL (good), and triglycerides. Your doctor uses this to calculate your heart disease risk and decide on medication or lifestyle changes.

recommendations.title: Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity. Offer or refer patients with prediabetes to effective preventive interventions.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 35–70 with overweight or obesity should be screened for diabetes and prediabetes with a fasting glucose or A1c test. If you have prediabetes, lifestyle changes and/or medication can delay or prevent type 2 diabetes.

recommendations.title: Obesity in Adults: Screening and Behavioral Interventions
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen all adults for obesity. Clinicians should offer or refer patients with a BMI of 30 or higher to intensive, multicomponent behavioral intervention programs.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults should have their BMI assessed at routine visits. If your BMI is 30 or above, your doctor should offer or refer you to an intensive behavioral weight loss program, which can significantly improve health outcomes.

recommendations.title: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for depression in the general adult population, including pregnant and postpartum persons. Adequate systems should be in place to ensure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate follow-up.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All adults should be screened for depression at routine visits. Common screening tools include the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9. Screening during and after pregnancy is especially important — perinatal depression is common and treatable.

recommendations.title: Anxiety Disorders in Adults: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for anxiety disorders in adults aged 18 to 64 years. Evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms for screening adults 65 years and older.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults aged 18–64 should be screened for anxiety disorders at routine visits. Common tools include the GAD-7 questionnaire. If you experience excessive worry, panic, or fear that interferes with daily life, discuss it with your doctor.

recommendations.title: Unhealthy Alcohol Use: Screening and Brief Counseling
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for unhealthy alcohol use in primary care settings in adults 18 years or older, including pregnant persons, and provide persons engaged in risky or hazardous drinking with brief behavioral counseling interventions.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All adults should be screened for unhealthy drinking patterns at routine visits. If you're drinking more than recommended (more than 14 drinks/week for men, more than 7 for women), a brief conversation with your doctor can help. Brief counseling is effective at reducing alcohol misuse.

recommendations.title: Drug Use in Adults: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen adults aged 18 years or older for unhealthy drug use in primary care settings when adequate treatment and follow-up care are available.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults should be asked about drug use at routine visits. If a problem is identified, your doctor can connect you with evidence-based treatments, including medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder.

recommendations.title: HIV Infection: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for HIV infection in adolescents and adults aged 15 to 65 years. Younger adolescents and adults older than 65 at increased risk should also be screened.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All adults and teens 15–65 should be screened for HIV at least once. People with ongoing risk factors — multiple partners, injection drug use, or an HIV-positive partner — should be screened at least annually. HIV is highly treatable when detected early.

recommendations.title: Hepatitis C Virus Infection: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in adults aged 18 to 79 years.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 18–79 should be screened for hepatitis C at least once. People born between 1945 and 1965 are at highest risk. HCV is now curable with a short course of oral medication.

recommendations.title: Hepatitis B Virus Infection: Screening in At-Risk Persons
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in adolescents and adults at increased risk, including persons born in countries with HBV prevalence of 2% or higher, U.S.-born persons not vaccinated as infants whose parents were born in regions with HBV prevalence of 8% or higher, and HIV-positive persons.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: People at increased risk for hepatitis B — including those born in or with parents from high-prevalence countries (East Asia, Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Eastern Europe) — should be screened with a blood test. Effective vaccines and treatments exist.

recommendations.title: Syphilis: Screening in Persons at Increased Risk
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for syphilis infection in persons who are at increased risk for infection, including men who have sex with men, people with HIV, those with multiple sexual partners, commercial sex workers, and persons with a prior STI.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: People at increased risk for syphilis should be screened regularly (at least annually). At-risk groups include men who have sex with men, people with HIV, and those with multiple sexual partners. Syphilis is easily cured with antibiotics if caught early.

recommendations.title: Chlamydia and Gonorrhea: Screening in Women
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhea in sexually active women 24 years or younger, and in women 25 years or older who are at increased risk for infection.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Sexually active women under 25 should be tested for chlamydia and gonorrhea every year. Women 25+ with multiple or new partners should also be screened. Both infections often have no symptoms but can cause infertility if untreated.

recommendations.title: Latent Tuberculosis Infection: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in populations at increased risk, including persons born in or who have lived in countries with high TB prevalence, those who currently or have previously lived in congregate settings such as prisons or shelters, and persons who are immunocompromised.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: People at increased risk for tuberculosis should be screened with a TB skin test (TST) or blood test (IGRA). Risk factors include being born in a high-TB country (Asia, Africa, Latin America), homelessness or prior incarceration, and weakened immunity. Treating latent TB prevents it from becoming active.

recommendations.title: Hepatitis B in Pregnant Women: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in pregnant women at their first prenatal visit.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All pregnant women should be tested for hepatitis B at the first prenatal visit. If positive, the newborn will receive hepatitis B vaccine and immune globulin at birth — highly effective at preventing transmission to the baby.

recommendations.title: HIV Infection in Pregnant Women: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for HIV infection in all pregnant persons, including those in labor who are untested and whose HIV status is unknown.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All pregnant women should be tested for HIV at the first prenatal visit. If HIV is detected, antiretroviral treatment can reduce the risk of transmission to the baby to near zero.

recommendations.title: Syphilis Infection in Pregnant Women: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for syphilis infection in all pregnant women.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All pregnant women should be tested for syphilis at the first prenatal visit and again in the third trimester if at increased risk. Untreated syphilis during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious illness in the newborn — but is easily cured with penicillin.

recommendations.title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for gestational diabetes mellitus in asymptomatic pregnant women at 24 weeks of gestation or after.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Pregnant women should be screened for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks with a 1-hour glucose challenge test. If elevated, a 3-hour glucose tolerance test is done to confirm. Treating gestational diabetes reduces risks for both mother and baby.

recommendations.title: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) Screening in Late Pregnancy
recommendations.recommendation_text: All pregnant women should be cultured for group B streptococcus (GBS) at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks of gestation.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Near the end of pregnancy (36–38 weeks), a swab test checks for Group B Strep bacteria. About 25% of women carry GBS harmlessly. If positive, IV antibiotics during labor protect the newborn from a potentially serious infection.

recommendations.title: Osteoporosis: Bone Density Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for osteoporosis with bone measurement testing (DEXA scan) in women 65 years or older. Screen postmenopausal women younger than 65 who are at increased risk as determined by a formal clinical risk assessment tool.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Women 65 and older should have a bone density (DEXA) scan to screen for osteoporosis. Younger postmenopausal women with risk factors — low body weight, smoking, family history of hip fracture, or long-term corticosteroid use — should also be screened.

recommendations.title: Intimate Partner Violence: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for intimate partner violence (IPV) in women of reproductive age and provide or refer women who screen positive to ongoing support services.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Women of reproductive age should be asked about intimate partner violence at clinical visits. If you are experiencing abuse, your doctor can connect you confidentially with support resources, safety planning, and counseling.

recommendations.title: Falls Prevention in Older Adults: Exercise Interventions
recommendations.recommendation_text: Prescribe exercise interventions to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults 65 years or older who are at increased risk for falls.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 65 and older at increased risk for falls should be offered exercise programs — especially balance training (tai chi, yoga) and strength training — to reduce fall risk. Falls are a leading cause of injury and death in older adults.

recommendations.title: Vision in Children Ages 3 to 5: Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen for amblyopia, strabismus, and visual acuity deficits in children aged 3 to 5 years to detect amblyopia or its risk factors.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Children should have vision screening before starting school, ideally at ages 3–5, to detect amblyopia (lazy eye) and strabismus (eye misalignment). When caught early, these conditions are highly treatable.

recommendations.title: Dental Caries Prevention in Children Under 5
recommendations.recommendation_text: Apply fluoride varnish to the primary teeth of all infants and children starting at the age of primary tooth eruption. Prescribe oral fluoride supplementation starting at 6 months for children whose water supply is deficient in fluoride.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Starting when the first tooth comes in, children should receive fluoride varnish applied by their primary care provider at well-child visits. Children in areas with low-fluoride water should also take fluoride drops or tablets to prevent tooth decay.

recommendations.title: A1c Monitoring in Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: Measure A1c at least twice yearly in patients with diabetes who are meeting treatment goals. Measure quarterly in patients whose glycemia is not at goal or whose therapy has changed.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes, your A1c (a 3-month average of blood sugar) should be checked at least twice a year when controlled, and every 3 months if not at goal or after a medication change. Target is typically below 7% for most adults.

recommendations.title: Annual Dilated Eye Exam in Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: In adults with type 2 diabetes, perform a dilated eye exam at diagnosis and at least annually thereafter. In adults with type 1 diabetes, begin dilated eye exams within 5 years of diagnosis, then annually. If retinopathy is well-controlled and absent, every 1–2 years may be considered.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes, get a dilated eye exam every year to check for diabetic retinopathy. This painless exam can detect early changes in the retina that, if untreated, can lead to vision loss. Early treatment is highly effective.

recommendations.title: Kidney Disease Monitoring in Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: In adults with type 2 diabetes, assess urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at diagnosis and at least annually. In adults with type 1 diabetes for 5 or more years, assess annually.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes, your kidneys should be checked every year with a urine test (uACR) and blood test (eGFR). Diabetic kidney disease develops silently — catching it early allows for medications that can dramatically slow its progression.

recommendations.title: Annual Comprehensive Foot Exam in Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: Perform a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually in all people with diabetes. Examine feet at every visit for patients with prior foot ulceration, prior amputation, or high-risk foot conditions including neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, or deformity.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes, get a foot exam at least once a year. Your doctor will check nerve function, circulation, and skin integrity. Report any sores, calluses, or numbness promptly — diabetic foot problems can escalate quickly but are often preventable.

recommendations.title: Vitamin D Deficiency Screening — Not Recommended
recommendations.recommendation_text: Do not screen asymptomatic, community-dwelling, nonpregnant adults for vitamin D deficiency. The harms of screening outweigh the benefits in asymptomatic adults.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Routine vitamin D blood testing is not recommended for healthy adults without symptoms — it has not been shown to improve health and can lead to unnecessary treatment. Testing may still be appropriate if you have symptoms or a condition affecting bone health; ask your doctor.

recommendations.title: Behavioral Counseling: Healthy Diet and Physical Activity for CVD Prevention
recommendations.recommendation_text: Offer or refer adults with cardiovascular disease risk factors to behavioral counseling interventions to promote a healthy diet and physical activity.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have risk factors for heart disease — such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, prediabetes, or obesity — your doctor should offer or refer you to counseling programs that help with healthy eating and physical activity. These programs measurably reduce heart disease risk.

recommendations.title: Weight Loss Interventions for Adults with Obesity
recommendations.recommendation_text: Offer or refer adults with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions that combine dietary changes, increased physical activity, and behavioral strategies, typically involving 12 or more sessions in the first year.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If your BMI is 30 or higher, your doctor should offer or refer you to an intensive weight loss program that combines nutrition guidance, physical activity, and behavior change support over multiple sessions. These programs lead to meaningful, sustained weight loss and health improvements.

recommendations.title: Hearing Loss in Older Adults: Screening (Insufficient Evidence)
recommendations.recommendation_text: The evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults 50 years or older.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: There is not enough evidence to say whether routine hearing screening helps adults 50 and older who have no symptoms. If you notice hearing difficulty — turning up the TV, asking people to repeat themselves, trouble in noisy rooms — tell your doctor; a hearing test and hearing aids can make a real difference.

recommendations.title: Cognitive Impairment in Older Adults: Screening (Insufficient Evidence)
recommendations.recommendation_text: The evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for cognitive impairment in community-dwelling adults 65 years or older who have no signs or symptoms of cognitive impairment.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: There is not enough evidence to recommend for or against routine memory screening in adults 65+ who have no symptoms. If you or your family notice memory lapses, confusion, or changes in thinking, raise it with your doctor — evaluation at that point is worthwhile.

recommendations.title: Thyroid Dysfunction: Screening (Insufficient Evidence)
recommendations.recommendation_text: The evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for thyroid dysfunction in nonpregnant, asymptomatic adults.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: There is not enough evidence to recommend routine thyroid blood testing for adults with no symptoms. If you have symptoms such as unexplained fatigue, weight change, feeling unusually cold or hot, or a family history of thyroid disease, ask your doctor whether a TSH test makes sense.

recommendations.title: Oral Health in Adults: Primary Care Screening and Preventive Interventions (Insufficient Evidence)
recommendations.recommendation_text: The evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine screening examinations and preventive interventions for oral health conditions performed by primary care clinicians in asymptomatic adults.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: There is not enough evidence to say whether primary care doctors should routinely screen healthy adults for dental problems. Regardless, regular dental check-ups and cleanings with a dentist remain the standard way to prevent tooth decay and gum disease.

recommendations.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Behavioral Counseling
recommendations.recommendation_text: Offer behavioral counseling for all sexually active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for sexually transmitted infections.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Sexually active teens and adults at increased STI risk — new or multiple partners, a partner with an STI, or inconsistent condom use — should be offered counseling on safer sex. Even brief counseling sessions reduce STI rates.

recommendations.title: Self-Measured Blood Pressure Monitoring at Home
recommendations.recommendation_text: Endorse the use of self-measured blood pressure (SMBP) monitoring, preferably combined with additional support (education, telemonitoring, or pharmacist-led care), to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension and to monitor blood pressure control during treatment.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Checking your blood pressure at home with a validated upper-arm cuff is endorsed by heart specialists. It helps confirm whether office readings are truly high and tracks how well treatment is working. Use a proper cuff, sit quietly for 5 minutes, and take readings at consistent times.

recommendations.title: Physical Activity: At Least 150 Minutes per Week
recommendations.recommendation_text: Adults should accumulate at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity activity, or an equivalent combination, spread throughout the week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days per week.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week — a brisk 30-minute walk 5 days a week counts — plus strength training twice a week. Even smaller amounts help; something is always better than nothing.

recommendations.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation After a Heart Event
recommendations.recommendation_text: Eligible patients — including those after myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, coronary artery bypass graft surgery, stable angina, heart valve repair or replacement, heart transplant, or chronic heart failure — should be referred to a comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation program. Referral is a Class I (strong) recommendation in AHA/ACC guidelines.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have had a heart attack, stent, bypass surgery, or have heart failure, ask your doctor for a referral to cardiac rehabilitation. These supervised programs combine exercise training, education, and support — and are proven to reduce the risk of another event and help you live longer. They are widely covered by insurance but often under-referred.

recommendations.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Insulin-Treated Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) should be offered for glycemic management in adults with type 1 diabetes, and in adults with type 2 diabetes who are on insulin therapy, including multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have type 1 diabetes, or type 2 diabetes treated with insulin, you should be offered a continuous glucose monitor — a small wearable sensor that tracks your glucose around the clock and alerts you to highs and lows. It improves control and reduces dangerous low blood sugar episodes.

recommendations.title: Annual Dental Exam for People with Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: People with diabetes should be referred for a thorough dental examination at least annually. Periodontal disease is more common and more severe in people with diabetes, and treatment of periodontal disease can improve glycemic outcomes.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes, see a dentist at least once a year for a full exam. Diabetes raises the risk of gum disease, and gum disease in turn makes blood sugar harder to control — treating it can actually improve your glucose levels.

recommendations.title: Diabetes Distress and Depression Screening in Diabetes
recommendations.recommendation_text: Routinely screen people with diabetes for diabetes distress, depression, anxiety, and disordered eating using validated tools, with referral to behavioral health professionals when indicated. Screening should occur at diagnosis, at regular intervals, and when there is a change in disease status or treatment.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Living with diabetes is demanding, and feeling burned out, overwhelmed, or depressed is common — your care team should ask about this regularly, not just at diagnosis. If the daily burden of diabetes feels heavy, tell your doctor; support and treatment genuinely help both mood and glucose control.

recommendations.title: Preconception Counseling Visit
recommendations.recommendation_text: All persons planning pregnancy should have a preconception care visit to review medical conditions, medications, immunization status, genetic and family history, substance use, and to initiate folic acid supplementation and optimize chronic disease control before conception.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you are thinking about becoming pregnant, schedule a preconception visit. Your clinician will review your health conditions and medications, update needed vaccines, check whether genetic carrier screening makes sense, and get you started on folic acid — all before you conceive, when it matters most.

recommendations.title: Annual Well-Woman Visit
recommendations.recommendation_text: Women should have at least one well-woman visit per year. The visit should include a review of medical, surgical, family, and social history; assessment of preventive service needs; and age-appropriate physical examination and screening, with services delivered across single or multiple visits as appropriate.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Plan a well-woman visit every year — even when you feel fine. It is a dedicated time to review your overall health, update recommended screenings, discuss contraception, menopause, or other concerns, and catch issues early.

recommendations.title: Cervical Cancer Screening Intervals (ACOG / ASCCP-Aligned)
recommendations.recommendation_text: For average-risk women aged 30–65, screen with cervical cytology every 3 years, primary hrHPV testing every 5 years, or co-testing (cytology plus hrHPV) every 5 years. Screening may be discontinued after age 65 with adequate prior negative screening.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: For ages 30–65, you can choose with your doctor: a Pap test every 3 years, an HPV test every 5 years, or both tests together every 5 years. All three are effective. After 65, screening can stop if your past results were consistently normal.

recommendations.title: Blood Pressure Screening at Every Prenatal Visit
recommendations.recommendation_text: Blood pressure should be measured at every prenatal visit to detect gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation warrants evaluation for preeclampsia, including assessment for proteinuria and signs of end-organ involvement.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Your blood pressure is checked at every prenatal visit for a reason — pregnancy-related high blood pressure and preeclampsia can develop quickly and silently. Report warning signs between visits too: severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, or sudden swelling.

recommendations.title: Postpartum Depression Screening
recommendations.recommendation_text: Screen all perinatal patients for depression and anxiety symptoms using a validated instrument (such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, EPDS) at least once during the perinatal period, including at the comprehensive postpartum visit (typically 4–6 weeks after delivery), with systems in place for follow-up diagnosis and treatment.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Postpartum depression affects about 1 in 8 new mothers and is treatable. Your care team should screen you with a short questionnaire around your 4–6 week postpartum visit. If you feel persistently sad, anxious, or overwhelmed after delivery, speak up — help works and you are not alone.

recommendations.title: Progesterone for Prevention of Recurrent Preterm Birth
recommendations.recommendation_text: Offer progesterone supplementation to pregnant persons with a singleton gestation and a prior spontaneous singleton preterm birth, to reduce the risk of recurrent preterm birth. Cervical length screening in the midtrimester can further identify candidates for vaginal progesterone.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you previously delivered a baby early (before 37 weeks) on its own and are pregnant again with a single baby, progesterone treatment can lower the chance of another early delivery. Ask your obstetrician whether this applies to you and discuss cervical length checks.

recommendations.title: Lung Cancer Screening — ACS (Annual LDCT, Ages 55–74)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Annual low-dose CT screening for adults aged 55 to 74 years in fairly good health who have at least a 30 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. Note: the USPSTF 2021 recommendation covers a broader group (ages 50–80 with a 20 pack-year history), and ACS updated its own guidance in 2023 to align with the broader criteria.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you are a current or former heavy smoker, ask about annual low-dose CT lung screening. The American Cancer Society's longstanding criteria covered ages 55–74 with a 30+ pack-year history; current criteria (like the USPSTF's) are broader — ages 50–80 with a 20 pack-year history. Your doctor can tell you if you qualify.

recommendations.title: Prostate Cancer Screening — ACS (Shared Decision-Making)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Asymptomatic men with at least a 10-year life expectancy should have an opportunity to make an informed decision with their healthcare provider about PSA screening, after receiving information about uncertainties, risks, and potential benefits. This discussion should begin at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for men at high risk (Black men or those with a first-degree relative diagnosed before age 65), and age 40 for men with more than one first-degree relative diagnosed at an early age.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Talk with your doctor about whether PSA prostate screening is right for you — starting at 50 for most men, 45 if you are Black or have a father or brother who had prostate cancer before 65, and 40 if multiple close relatives were diagnosed young. The decision is yours to make with full information on benefits and harms.
